desc:
There are n employees numbered 0..n-1 and one round table. Employee i has a favorite colleague favorite[i] (never themselves). The company invites some employees and seats them around the table in any order of its choosing. An invited employee attends only if they are seated directly next to their favorite colleague, on the left or on the right (a table with two people counts both neighbours as the same person).

Return the largest number of employees that can be invited and seated so that everybody invited is happy. The favorite of an invited employee must of course be invited too.

Example: favorite = [2, 2, 1, 2] returns 3: invite 0, 1 and 2 and seat them as 0, 2, 1 around the table. Employee 3 cannot join.
hints: Treat i -> favorite[i] as an arrow. Every employee has exactly one outgoing arrow, so each connected piece is a cycle with chains of employees leading into it.

At a round table everyone must sit beside their favorite. For a cycle of three or more employees the only way to satisfy everyone in it is to seat the whole cycle in order, and nobody else fits. A 2-cycle (two employees who like each other) is different: other people can sit on the outer sides of these two.

Answer = max(longest cycle of length ≥ 3, total over all 2-cycles of [2 + longest chain leading into one member + longest chain leading into the other]). Find chain lengths by repeatedly removing employees nobody likes (topological order), propagating the depth along the arrows.
editorial: Each component of the arrow graph has exactly one cycle. If the table contains someone from a cycle of length L ≥ 3, their favorite and the favorite's favorite follow the arrows and force all L employees in order around the table; no free seat remains, so the table consists of that cycle alone. The candidate is L.

For a 2-cycle (a, b) the table can be built as a line that runs ... -> a, b <- ...: a chain of employees x1 -> x2 -> ... -> a sits to one side of a, and a chain leading into b sits on the other side of b, and the two ends of this line meet around the table. Different 2-cycles can share the same table, because the line from one 2-cycle can close up with the line of another. So all 2-cycles are added up, each contributing 2 plus the longest chain entering each of its members.

Computing it: count in-degrees, put all employees with in-degree 0 in a queue, pop one and relax depth[favorite[u]] = max(depth[favorite[u]], depth[u] + 1) (all depths start at 1), decrease in-degree of the target and push it when it hits 0. The employees that never get popped are exactly the cycle members. Walk each cycle once: for L ≥ 3 update the best length, for L = 2 add depth[a] + depth[b] to the 2-cycle total. The result is the maximum of the two. All steps are O(n).
